{{Short description|Specific class of fifteen prime numbers}}
In [[moonshine theory]], a '''supersingular prime''' is a [[prime number]] that [[divisor|divides]] the [[Order (group theory)|order]] of the [[Monster group]] <math>M</math>, which is the largest [[sporadic simple group]]. There are precisely fifteen supersingular prime numbers: the first eleven primes [[2 (number)|2]], [[3 (number)|3]], [[5 (number)|5]], [[7 (number)|7]], [[11 (number)|11]], [[13 (number)|13]], [[17 (number)|17]], [[19 (number)|19]], [[23 (number)|23]], [[29 (number)|29]], and [[31 (number)|31]]; as well as [[41 (number)|41]], [[47 (number)|47]], [[59 (number)|59]], and [[71 (number)|71]] {{OEIS|id=A002267}}.

The non-supersingular primes are [[37 (number)|37]], [[43 (number)|43]], [[53 (number)|53]], [[61 (number)|61]], [[67 (number)|67]], and all primes greater than or equal to [[73 (number)|73]].

This usage of "supersingular prime" should not be confused with the related but distinct notion from [[algebraic number theory]]. In that context, a prime is called [[supersingular prime (algebraic number theory)|supersingular ''for'' a given elliptic curve <math>E</math>]] if reducing <math>E</math> modulo <math>p</math> yields a [[supersingular elliptic curve]]—a property that depends on the choice of curve, and every elliptic curve over <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> has infinitely many such primes. By contrast, the fifteen supersingular primes defined here are not relative to any particular curve: they are characterized by a condition on ''all'' supersingular elliptic curves in characteristic <math>p</math> at once (see [[#Characterization|below]]), and happen to coincide with the prime divisors of the order of the Monster group.

== Characterization ==

[[Andrew Ogg]] (1975) proved that a prime number <math>p</math> satisfies the following equivalent conditions:{{sfn|Ogg|1980}}

# The [[modular curve]] <math>X_0^+(p) = X_0(p)/w_p</math>, the quotient of <math>X_0(p)</math> by the [[Fricke involution]] <math>w_p</math>, has [[geometric genus|genus]] zero.
# Every [[supersingular elliptic curve]] in characteristic <math>p</math> can be defined over the [[prime subfield]] <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math>.
# <math>p</math> is one of the fifteen primes listed above.

The connection to elliptic curves arises through condition (2). For any prime <math>p</math>, there are only finitely many [[j-invariant|<math>j</math>-invariants]] of supersingular elliptic curves in characteristic <math>p</math>; these <math>j</math>-invariants are the roots of the '''supersingular polynomial''' <math>ss_p(X) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X]</math>, and there are approximately <math>p/12</math> of them (see [[supersingular elliptic curve]]).{{sfn|Silverman|2009|pp=V §4}} In general, these <math>j</math>-invariants may lie in extensions of <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> (specifically in <math>\mathbb{F}_{p^2}</math>). Condition (2) states that for the fifteen supersingular primes—and only for these primes—every supersingular <math>j</math>-invariant already lies in <math>\mathbb{F}_p</math> itself. For larger primes, some supersingular <math>j</math>-invariants necessarily require the quadratic extension <math>\mathbb{F}_{p^2}</math>.

The equivalence of conditions (1) and (2) is a result in the arithmetic geometry of modular curves: the supersingular points on <math>X_0(p)</math> in characteristic <math>p</math> correspond to supersingular elliptic curves with a cyclic <math>p</math>-isogeny, and the genus of the quotient curve <math>X_0^+(p)</math> controls whether all such points can be rational.{{sfn|Ogg|1980}}

== Role in monstrous moonshine ==

Shortly after establishing the equivalence of conditions (1) and (2), Ogg attended a talk by [[Jacques Tits]] in which the [[conjecture]]d existence of a sporadic simple group—later constructed as the [[Monster group]] by [[Robert Griess]] in 1982—was described, along with its predicted order. Ogg noticed that the prime factors of this predicted order were exactly the fifteen primes on his list, and offered a bottle of [[Jack Daniel's]] whiskey for an explanation of the coincidence.{{sfn|Ogg|1980}} This observation, connecting the arithmetic of modular curves to the representation theory of sporadic groups, was one of the motivating problems for the theory of [[Moonshine theory|monstrous moonshine]], later developed by [[John Horton Conway|Conway]] and [[Simon P. Norton|Norton]] (1979) and proved by [[Richard Borcherds]] (1992).

== Other properties ==

All fifteen supersingular primes are [[Chen prime]]s, but 37, 53, and 67 are also Chen primes without being supersingular, and there are infinitely many Chen primes greater than 73.
